Finite Euler-product identities

These are identities for the Dirichlet-convolution square μ*μ\mu*\mu, not the pointwise square μ(n)2\mu(n)^2. For each prime pp, its coefficients at 1,p,p21,p,p^2 are 1,−2,11,-2,1, and the higher prime-power coefficients vanish. The local factors at exponents 11 and 22 are 1−2p+1p2=(1−1p)2,1−2p2+1p4=(1−1p2)2.1-\frac2p+\frac1{p^2}=\left(1-\frac1p\right)^2, \qquad 1-\frac2{p^2}+\frac1{p^4}=\left(1-\frac1{p^2}\right)^2. For a prime pp and e≥0e\ge0, the corresponding convolution with the divisor-sum function σ\sigma gives σ(pe+2)−2σ(pe+1)+σ(pe)=pe+1(p−1)=φ(pe+2).\sigma(p^{e+2})-2\sigma(p^{e+1})+\sigma(p^e) =p^{e+1}(p-1)=\varphi(p^{e+2}). This follows by subtracting the finite geometric sums. These finite identities do not assert a transcendence result. Parameter ranges and quantifiers

The distinction between a finite calculation and an unbounded family is in the quantifiers. A statement such as ∀a≥8\forall a\ge8 is uniform in aa, whereas a list of computed scales is finite and a condition ∀N0∃N≥N0\forall N_0\,\exists N\ge N_0 asks for witnesses arbitrarily far out. The table uses these distinctions even when a uniform statement is conditional on an unproved hypothesis. A bound on a secondary variable, such as J+(a+6)<2⋅2aJ+(a+6)<2\cdot2^a in the positivity row, does not bound aa.

Some identities have no distinguished scale parameter. They are listed with the general identities. An equivalence can hold for all parameters without establishing either of the equivalent arithmetic assertions.

The LCM formulation of Problem 249 requires arbitrarily large scales: irrational_totientSeries_iff_actualLcmOrbitNonintegralitySupply Irrational(∑n≥1φ(n)/2n)⇔∀a0∃a≥a0,Ωa∉ℤ,\mathrm{Irrational}\Bigl(\sum_{n\ge 1}\varphi(n)/2^n\Bigr) \iff \forall a_0\ \exists a\ge a_0,\ \Omega_a \notin \mathbb Z, a cofinal statement in the exponent aa indexing H=H(2a)H=H(2^a). A finite calculation alone does not establish it; a further theorem could propagate finite information to arbitrarily large scales.

The table groups statements by their parameter ranges, not by proof status. In particular, some assertions with cofinal quantifiers are already proved, such as the prime constructions and rational comparison sequences. Others are implications whose quantified hypotheses remain open. The horizontal rule separates the cofinal group for ease of reference; it does not mark a boundary between proved and unproved mathematics. The descriptions identify this distinction in that group. The prefixes summarise the quantifiers; complete hypotheses are given in the cited statements. A definition records an object or condition; it does not by itself prove the associated soundness or existence assertion.

In the periodic-weight rows, write w:ℕ→ℤw:\mathbb N\to\mathbb Z and cw(n)=∑d∣nw(d)c_w(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}w(d) for n≥1n\ge1. Positivity and nonvanishing refer to these divisor coefficients, not to the weight ww itself. Here “nonzero arbitrarily far out” means that for every NN there is n>Nn>N with cw(n)≠0c_w(n)\ne0; it does not mean nonvanishing on every arithmetic progression. The nonprincipal character χ4\chi_4 modulo four is 00 on even integers and (−1)(n−1)/2(-1)^{(n-1)/2} on odd integers.

Finite extension and cofinal estimates

Extending a computation supplies more finite witnesses. To reach a cofinal statement, an argument must instead produce a witness beyond an arbitrary threshold. The examples below specify which of these extensions is needed; the largest computed scale is not asserted to be a limit of the method.

  1. Finite certificate tables. Results such as the diagonal certificates at 28 explicit values of tt through t=64t{=}64, now a strict subset of the aggregate band t≤82t\le82 (certifiedKill_diagonal_all_imported), the certificates for h∈[1,8]h\in[1,8] at fixed depth 16 (certifiedKill_all_small), and the exclusions for h∈[1,16]h\in[1,16] at exponent 14 (totient_series_ne_rat_of_den_dvd_pow_two_mul_mersenne_upto_sixteen) are each a finite list of independently verified rows, not a single argument instantiated at a free parameter. The existing lists do not establish further rows; an extension needs either additional computations or an argument for a family of parameters.

  2. A bounded window inside a uniform theorem. The rough-integer bound of Proposition 6.79 and the positivity theorem of Proposition 6.84 hold for every a≥8a\ge8, subject to their stated bounds on the other parameters. In the sign theorem, for example, J+a+6<2⋅2aJ+a+6<2\cdot2^a. Their proofs are therefore not merely enumerations of a fixed set of exponents. The missing conclusion is a suitable residue inequality at arbitrarily large scales, not extension of the range of aa in the positivity theorem. No complexity lower bound follows from these examples.

  3. Parameter dependence in an approximation estimate. For reduced approximants pK/qKp_K/q_K to SS, the conditions 0<|S−pK/qK|≤εK0<|S-p_K/q_K|\le\varepsilon_K and qKεK→0q_K\varepsilon_K\to0 imply irrationality. A growing denominator alone does not control this product. In particular, the exact reduced-denominator formula of Proposition 6.8 concerns a specified finite Möbius sum; it does not estimate the complementary tail. Likewise, a bound proved with a constant depending on a fixed auxiliary parameter is not automatically uniform when that parameter grows. Both the dependence of the constant and the error estimate must be retained in any passage to an unbounded family.

The missing arithmetic inputs include the stated constant-saving exponential-sum estimate and an upper-endpoint residue inequality. For the positivity theorem, the unresolved step is exclusion of that residue interval, not positivity at more exponents.

Relations between the representations

Binary tails, Möbius sums, rational approximations and exponential sums express related information about SS. We give the identities that connect them and then check which assumptions survive each change. This is necessary before transferring a counterexample to another representation, as the finite-state decoding and polynomial denominator examples illustrate.

Binary-weighted series and tails.

The coefficients in S=∑n≥1φ(n)2−nS=\sum_{n\ge1}\varphi(n)2^{-n} are unbounded; this expression is not the base-two digit expansion of SS. The tail RNR_N, finite difference numerator D(h,N,L)D(h,N,L) and test 𝒞(h,N,L)\mathcal C(h,N,L) retain this coefficient information. The identity S=12+∑d≥1μ(d)(2d−1)2S=\frac12+\sum_{d\ge1}\frac{\mu(d)}{(2^d-1)^2} (tsum_totient_half_pow_eq_half_add_moebius_sq) and its partial-sum version (mobius_square_series_eq_partial_add_tail) express the same value by Möbius sums. An equality of values does not by itself transfer a claim about the original coefficient subsequences.

Lambert sums and finite numerator polynomials.

The Lambert identities for μ\mu, 11 and φ\varphi give the series relations in Section 5. For a finite divisor sum, the polynomial evaluation (mobiusNumeratorPolynomial_eval_two) and the definition (mobiusNumerator) put its numerator into integer polynomial arithmetic. This evaluates a finite contribution, not the complementary infinite tail.

Coprimality probability.

Let X,YX,Y be independent with Pr⁡(X=n)=Pr⁡(Y=n)=2−n\Pr(X=n)=\Pr(Y=n)=2^{-n} for n≥1n\ge1. Then S−12=Pr⁡(gcd⁡(X,Y)=1)S-\tfrac12=\Pr(\gcd(X,Y)=1). The divisibility probabilities are Pr⁡(d∣X,d∣Y)=(2d−1)−2\Pr(d\mid X,\ d\mid Y)=(2^d-1)^{-2} (tsum_pos_pair_both_dvd_half_eq_inv_mersenne_sq). Möbius inversion converts these to the coprimality probability. The decomposition by the greatest common divisor also gives the weighted coprime-pair identity (tsum_pos_coprime_inv_mersenne_eq_one). Counting coprime pairs by their sum gives the totient expression directly (tsum_coprime_pair_pow_eq_tsum_totient_mul_pow).

Cyclotomic factors of finite denominators.

The coefficient formula for PrP_r (mobiusNumeratorPolynomial_coeff) and the cyclotomic divisibility statement (cyclotomicValue_dvd_baseMobiusShadow_den) identify factors in the reduced denominators of the specified finite sums. The product-divisibility theorem (upperHalfChannel_product_dvd_den_of_scale_primeFactors_le) is used in the exact denominator formula (lcmHeight_scaledMobiusShadow_den_exact). Growing finite denominators alone do not exclude cancellation with the remaining tail.

Numerator divisibility and denominator bounds.

Write x=a/bx=a/b in lowest terms, with b>0b>0. For c∈ℤc\in\mathbb{Z} and a positive divisor HH of bb, if the reduced denominator of cxcx divides HH, then b/H∣cb/H\mid c (scalarLocalization_complement_dvd). In particular, |c|≥b/H|c|\ge b/H when c≠0c\ne0. A related bound is 0<ab<22n−1,2r∣a,n≥1⇒2r(2n−1)<2b0<\frac ab<\frac2{2^n-1},\quad 2^r\mid a,\quad n\ge1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 2^r(2^n-1)<2b for integers r≥0r\ge0 (positiveRat_mersenne_height). Here positivity gives a≥2ra\ge2^r; the size inequality then gives the conclusion. These are arithmetic bounds on a reduced fraction, not irrationality criteria without an additional approximation estimate.

Farey intervals.

The denominator bound (farey_gap) applied to the explicit window (N,K)=(1,240)(N,K)=(1,240) gives (gap_check_window_1_240_le_79639646646701375323355774875831053) and hence S≠p/qS\ne p/q for integers pp and 1≤q≤Q01\le q\le Q_0. The finite input is a totient numerator modulo 22402^{240}. Its exact first failing denominator is Q0+1Q_0+1, the denominator of the relevant Farey mediant (gap_check_window_1_240_first_failure). This last assertion concerns this fixed window.

Differences at least-common-multiple shifts.

For Ht=lcm⁡(1,…,t)H_t=\operatorname{lcm}(1,\ldots,t) (periodLcm), a jump in HtH_t can occur only at a prime power (eq_prime_pow_of_not_dvd_periodLcm). The identities (lcmRayArithmeticLetter_eq_deltaTotient) and (diagonalWindowIncrement_eq_lcmRayArithmeticLetter) identify the coefficient difference as δt(j)=φ(2Ht+j)−φ(Ht+j)\delta_t(j)=\varphi(2H_t+j)-\varphi(H_t+j) and give D(Ht,Ht,L)=∑j=1Lδt(j)2L−jD(H_t,H_t,L)=\sum_{j=1}^L\delta_t(j)2^{L-j}. Thus these arithmetic formulas concern particular instances of the same finite residue test; additional window restrictions remain in force.

Exponential sums of the window residues.

For integers h,X≥1h,X\ge1, the relevant block statistic is ∑N=X2X−1cos⁡(2πD(h,N,L)2L).\sum_{N=X}^{2X-1}\cos\!\left(2\pi\frac{D(h,N,L)}{2^L}\right). A bound by 9X/109X/10, together with L≥hL\ge h and 16(2X+h+L+2)≤2L16(2X+h+L+2)\le2^L, yields a certificate in the block (exists_certifiedKill_of_first_harmonic_gap). The linked irrationality implication uses the stronger complex norm bound 21X/2521X/25, for every hh on arbitrarily late blocks satisfying the same size inequality (irrational_totient_series_of_first_harmonic_norm_gap). The finite implication uses cos⁡(π/8)>9/10\cos(\pi/8)>9/10; the required cancellation bound is still unproved. The norm bound on the complex exponential sum is sufficient for the displayed real-part bound, but is stronger.

Binary tails and Möbius sums

Erdős’s argument for ∑n1/(2n−1)\sum_n1/(2^n-1) chooses congruences so that divisor counts along a block are divisible by increasing powers of the base. A tail bound then forces a long run of zero digits [11]. It uses no finite automaton.

A different proposal would recover each later block from a fixed finite summary of the preceding history. The counterexample of Proposition 2.11(i) (balancedPulse_no_autonomous_decoder) shows why that proposal fails for the family constructed there. For m≥2m\ge2, its members have the same earlier history but different successors. A state that identifies all those histories cannot recover every successor. More generally, an exact label-and-decoder pair for that family needs at least ⌊(m+1)/2⌋+1\lfloor(m+1)/2\rfloor+1 distinct labels. This is a lower bound on the number of labels, not a linear lower bound on the number of bits, and it is not a state-complexity theorem for the actual totient sequence.

The implication from the quantified certificate condition (irrational_totient_series_of_certificate_supply) is a separate theorem. The counterexample above neither proves its hypothesis nor makes it the only possible route to irrationality. Likewise, Proposition 10.4 shows that inverse-phase column weights can preserve a determinant, and Theorem 6.3 gives the exact growing ranks of totient sections. These are different statements with different hypotheses; none is a general prohibition on other representations of SS.

The Möbius representation instead allows the squared-Lambert identity of Proposition 5.16 to be applied to μ\mu, since |μ(d)|≤d|\mu(d)|\le d for d≥1d\ge1. The polynomial identities of Propositions 6.37–6.41 operate at each finite radical without an autonomous decoder. The exact reduced denominator and its lower bound are then given by Propositions 6.8 and 6.7. Those formulas concern a finite rational contribution. They do not exclude cancellation by the complementary tail and hence do not settle irrationality. The representations are equal expressions for SS; what differs is the information supplied by the particular arguments.

Index of unproved conditions

Every condition in this index is accompanied by the implication that would turn it into irrationality of S=∑n≥0φ(n)2−nS=\sum_{n\ge0}\varphi(n)2^{-n}. Those implications are proved. The arithmetic hypotheses still have to be established with the displayed quantifiers.

Scope of the index

The index compares particular quantified hypotheses and the results that use them. An unsuccessful implication between two entries therefore says nothing by itself about every argument using the same method.

Each entry states its quantifiers in full. A cofinal assertion, with a quantifier of the form ∀a0∃a≥a0\forall a_0\ \exists a\ge a_0, may itself be proved or may remain an unproved hypothesis; the text of each entry says which. A cofinal assertion about a different quantity, or with a different order of quantifiers, need not supply the irrationality condition.

The quantified residue condition for #249, stated in Definition 1.2 and proved sufficient (irrational_totient_series_of_certificate_supply), is the following statement: ∀h≥1,∀N0,∃N≥N0,∃L,𝒞hNL.\forall h \ge 1,\ \forall N_0,\ \exists N \ge N_0,\ \exists L,\ \mathcal{C}\ h\ N\ L . The following catalogue compares fourteen proposed approaches to this condition. It starts with the exponential-sum estimate, then gives thirteen further approaches with their individual hypotheses and source references.

The exponential-sum criterion

We express the truncated tail difference as a phase and ask for cancellation when that phase is summed over a block. The following implications explain how a saving gives a residue certificate and, with the required quantifiers, Definition 1.2.

Definition 9.1 (The truncated difference). For h,N,L∈ℕh,N,L\in\mathbb N, D(h,N,L)=∑j=0L−1(φ(N+h+1+j)−φ(N+1+j))⋅2L−1−j∈ℤ.D(h,N,L) \;=\; \sum_{j=0}^{L-1} \bigl(\varphi(N+h+1+j) - \varphi(N+1+j)\bigr)\cdot 2^{\,L-1-j} \ \in \mathbb Z . This is the depth-LL truncation of 2L⋅(RN+h−RN)2^L\cdot(R_{N+h}-R_N), where RN=∑j≥1φ(N+j)/2jR_N = \sum_{j\ge 1}\varphi(N+j)/2^j is the local totient tail (totientTail). windowDiscrepancy

Definition 9.2 (The central-residue condition). 𝒞hNL:⇔(N+h+L+2)<D(h,N,L)mod⁡2L<2L−(N+h+L+2).\mathcal{C}\ h\ N\ L \;:\Leftrightarrow\; (N{+}h{+}L{+}2) < D(h,N,L)\operatorname{mod} 2^L < 2^L - (N{+}h{+}L{+}2). That is: the residue of D(h,N,L)D(h,N,L) modulo 2L2^L avoids the radius-(N+h+L+2)(N{+}h{+}L{+}2) neighbourhood of 00. It forces the size condition 2(N+h+L+2)<2L2(N{+}h{+}L{+}2) < 2^L (certifiedKill_depth_floor). certifiedKill

Definition 9.3 (The complex phase and its real part). Put Re⁡E(h,N,L)=cos⁡(2πD(h,N,L)mod⁡2L2L),E(h,N,L)=exp⁡(i2πD(h,N,L)mod⁡2L2L).\operatorname{Re}E(h,N,L) = \cos\!\Bigl(2\pi\,\tfrac{D(h,N,L)\operatorname{mod} 2^L}{2^L}\Bigr),\qquad E(h,N,L) = \exp\!\Bigl(i\,2\pi\,\tfrac{D(h,N,L)\operatorname{mod} 2^L}{2^L}\Bigr). The real part of EE is the displayed cosine (windowFirstExp_re), and |E(h,N,L)|=1|E(h,N,L)| = 1 (norm_windowFirstExp). Thus EE is the first additive character of the endpoint discrepancy modulo 2L2^L, a standard exponential-sum object. windowFirstCos windowFirstExp

Theorem 9.4 (A real-part bound gives a certificate). For all h,X,Lh,X,L with 0<X0<X and the size condition 16(2X+h+L+2)≤2L16(2X{+}h{+}L{+}2)\le 2^L, if ∑N=X2X−1Re⁡E(h,N,L)≤910X,\sum_{N=X}^{2X-1} \operatorname{Re}E(h,N,L) \;\le\; \tfrac{9}{10}\,X , then ∃N∈[X,2X)\exists N\in[X,2X) with 𝒞hNL\mathcal{C}\ h\ N\ L.

Theorem 9.5 (The same implication for a nonempty subset). For any nonempty finite T⊆ℕT\subseteq\mathbb N with T⊂[0,2X)T\subset[0,2X) and the same size condition, if ∑N∈TRe⁡E(h,N,L)≤910|T|,\sum_{N\in T} \operatorname{Re}E(h,N,L) \;\le\; \tfrac{9}{10}\,|T| , then ∃N∈T\exists N\in T with 𝒞hNL\mathcal{C}\ h\ N\ L. This generalises Theorem 9.4: TT can be any explicitly chosen nonempty finite subset of the dyadic block, not the whole block, and the proof (an averaging pigeonhole) never uses that TT has positive density or comes from a partition.

Theorem 9.6 (A norm bound gives the real-part criterion). The complex norm bound implies the real-part bound (|z|≥Re(z)|z|\ge\mathrm{Re}(z), and 21/25<9/1021/25 < 9/10 absorbs the slack), so it composes through Theorem 9.4 to the same certificate. Define block norm condition:⇔∀h>0∀X0∃X,L,max⁡(X0,1)≤X∧16(2X+h+L+2)≤2L∧\text{block norm condition} :\Leftrightarrow\; \forall h{>}0\ \forall X_0\ \exists X, L,\ \max(X_0,1)\le X\ \wedge\ 16(2X{+}h{+}L{+}2)\le 2^L\ \wedge ∥∑N=X2X−1E(h,N,L)∥≤2125X.\Bigl\|\ \sum_{N=X}^{2X-1}E(h,N,L)\ \Bigr\| \;\le\; \tfrac{21}{25}\,X . Then block norm condition⇒Irrational(∑n≥0φ(n)2n),\text{block norm condition} \;\Longrightarrow\; \mathrm{Irrational}\Bigl(\sum_{n\ge 0} \tfrac{\varphi(n)}{2^n}\Bigr), proved in full, with no further gap, by chaining Theorem 9.6→\toTheorem 9.4→\to Theorem 6.47.

Observation 9.7 (What remains unproved). The implications above do not establish the cofinal block estimate. Three further Lean statements retain a separation or gap hypothesis: one uses the two-element set {N,M}\{N,M\} (AdjacentPhaseSeparation.lean), and the other two use a supplied finite set TT and the singleton {N}\{N\} (PivotAntiReconstruction.lean, PivotAntiReconstruction.lean). They prove what follows from the relevant estimate; they do not provide that estimate at arbitrarily large scales. The finite numerical observations in Table [tab:blocks] are a different kind of evidence and do not discharge this quantified hypothesis.

Remark 9.8 (What the reduction does and does not prove). The required savings are explicit: a real-part bound of 9X/109X/10, or the stronger norm bound of 21X/2521X/25, on blocks at arbitrarily large scales for every positive shift hh. An unspecified nonzero saving is not the stated hypothesis. A bound o(X)o(X) would suffice, but it is more than the implication needs.

The inequality 16(2X+h+L+2)≤2L16(2X+h+L+2)\le2^L can be met by increasing LL for fixed X,hX,h. Doing so changes the exponential sum, and hence does not preserve an estimate proved at another depth. The arithmetic estimate must hold at a depth satisfying this inequality.

The subset theorem permits any nonempty finite sample inside [0,2X)[0,2X); no density assumption is required. A prime-defined sample is one possible choice. The four-term decomposition of §3.2 isolates one prime factor and the remaining totient-dependent phase, but does not prove the required cancellation between them.

Proved results and the additional assumptions they need

Besides the exponential-sum condition, the sufficient hypotheses involve tail signs, endpoint residues, rational approximation, short windows, Farey bounds, divisibility, denominator growth and carry rank. For each, we state the missing estimate used by the proposed application. These are specific possibilities rather than a classification of methods for Problem #249.

The fixed Farey bound

Theorem 9.30. If SS is rational, its reduced denominator exceeds 7.9639646646701375323355774875831053×10347.963\,964\,664\,670\,137\,532\,335\allowbreak\,577\,487\,583\,105\,3\times 10^{34}. This is the finite denominator exclusion in the corpus, logically independent of the certificate-supply reduction.

Remark 9.31 (What a larger Farey bound requires). Unbounded valid denominator exclusions would imply S∉ℚS\notin\mathbb{Q}. For the single window K=240K=240, however, the first-failure computation (gap_check_window_1_240_first_failure) proves that the residue inequality fails at the mediant denominator b+d=Q0+1b+d=Q_0+1. This exact first failure prevents a larger cutoff from that same inequality at that same window. It is not an obstruction to other windows or to other tests using the finite data.

The existing proofs for individual windows use explicit totient residues and rational endpoint calculations. Extending that implementation calls for new finite data; a uniform proof of a growing bound need not use hard-coded convergents. If SS had reduced denominator qq, every valid exclusion bound would be smaller than qq. Thus unbounded exclusions suffice for irrationality; rationality would bound them, but would not force eventual constancy. No converse or comparison with the continued-fraction denominators of SS is proved here.

Observation 9.32 (The limited gain from a unit-gap refinement). The finite unit-gap condition of Observation 6.114 (ReducedDenominatorUnitGapCert) and its quantified version (PrimitiveReducedDenominatorUnitGapSupply) are definitions; the latter is not asserted to hold. Two separate results (reducedDenominatorUnitGapCert_prime_pow_iff, reducedDenominatorCandidateCount_prime_pow_le_one) show that, for pp prime and e≥1e\ge1, a window at denominator pep^e that passes the refined test contains at most one candidate integer. A window with two or more candidates fails the test. This is a condition for successful certification, not a bound on all windows or on the improvement in the denominator cutoff. It does not apply to all odd denominators: Observation 6.114 gives an actual totient window with two admissible nonunit candidates modulo 1515.

Proposition 9.33 (A sufficient extension). Suppose g(K)→∞g(K)\to\infty and, for every KK, the (N=1,K)(N=1,K) gap check excludes every rational of reduced denominator at most g(K)g(K). Then SS is irrational: any rational value of SS would have a fixed finite denominator, contradicted at a sufficiently large KK. Only unbounded exclusion bounds along a sequence of windows are needed for this argument. No equivalence with a bound for the continued-fraction denominators of SS is asserted; such a comparison would require its own proof connecting those convergents to the certified intervals.

Remark 9.45 (Growth of these denominators does not give approximation of SS). The number HtβHtH_t\beta_{H_t} is the finite rational contribution to a totient-tail decomposition. Its complementary term can still cancel its fractional part. The stated denominator bound supplies neither an error estimate for approximation of SS nor nonintegrality of R2Ht−RHtR_{2H_t}-R_{H_t}.

To apply the diagonal criterion in Theorem 6.49, one must establish this tail nonintegrality at arbitrarily large LCM scales. Denominator growth alone does not supply that condition.

An upper bound tending to zero for this product is needed. A lower bound for the denominator cannot establish it; improving a lower bound does not change the actual approximation error.

A different argument could deduce a residue certificate from the surviving divisor and further information about the complementary term. The denominator theorem alone contains no such separation statement. Neither sufficient argument is established by its lower bound, and these are not claimed to exhaust possible approaches.

Rationality and carry rank

The totient sections have a dimension lower bound, as do the sections of an integral carry under the rationality hypothesis. An incompatible upper bound would finish a rank argument. The rational comparison sequences show why rationality by itself gives no such bound.

Theorem 9.47. For every e≥1e\ge1, the retained dyadic totient sections form a basis for all sections through level ee, of dimension 2e+12^e+1. The proof uses the Chinese remainder theorem and Dirichlet’s theorem. The complete level-zero truncation, consisting only of φ\varphi, has dimension one.

Theorem 9.48. If S∈ℚS\in\mathbb{Q}, choose an integer v>0v>0 with vS∈ℤvS\in\mathbb{Z} and put uN=vRNu_N=vR_N. Then uN∈ℤu_N\in\mathbb{Z}, uN+1=2uN−vφ(N+1)u_{N+1}=2u_N-v\varphi(N+1), and 0≤uN≤v(N+2)0\le u_N\le v(N+2). For every e≥0e\ge0, dim⁡ℚspan⁡{n↦u2jn+r:1≤j≤e,0≤r<2j}≥2e−1.\dim_{\mathbb{Q}}\operatorname{span} \{n\mapsto u_{2^j n+r}:1\le j\le e,\ 0\le r<2^j\}\ge2^e-1. The proof is given in Section 10.8.

Remark 9.49 (The generic upper-bound inference is false). The bound 2e−12^e-1 holds at every level. An upper bound contradicting it would need additional information about the totient, since the rational 5/45/4 comparison has the same lower bound. One proposed system of integer equalities and strict inequalities is inconsistent: there are no integers Q,v>0Q,v>0, A≠0A\ne0 and bb with QvA=bQvA=b and |b|<Qv|b|<Qv, since a nonzero integer multiple of QvQv has absolute value at least QvQv (false_of_compressedAdjointCertificate). This excludes those simultaneous requirements, not every argument using a matrix or its adjugate. Separately, the span of all dyadic totient sections is infinite-dimensional (Proposition 1.6).

Proposition 9.50 (An additional hypothesis for a totient-specific rank argument). A rank bound that contradicts the lower bound 2e−12^e-1 would have to use additional arithmetic of the actual totient coefficients. The generic proposal that rationality bounds the rank of every integral carry satisfying u(n)/2n→0u(n)/2^n\to0 is disproved by the comparison sequence recorded in the short paper: its carry rank is at least 2e−12^e-1 at every level. It is therefore not a remaining general lemma from which totient irrationality follows. The conditional Proposition 1.7 records eventual periodicity modulo vv together with unbounded rational rank. Periodicity of the residue sequences concerns values in a finite quotient; it does not bound the rational span of the integer-valued sections. The 5/45/4 comparison shows that this distinction persists for a rational coefficient series.

Relations between the sufficient conditions

A fixed saving for the real part or norm of the block exponential sum would give a certificate. The endpoint conditions seek a residue or size bound along an LCM sequence instead. Proposition 9.14 relates the sufficient formulations; the arithmetic estimates required by them remain open.

The generic bounded-rank argument fails for a separate reason: the rational comparison sequence has unbounded section rank. A totient-specific upper bound would require hypotheses not shared by that sequence.

These are statements about the displayed conditions and comparisons, not an exhaustive classification of possible proofs. Some conditions are equivalent to irrationality; others are only sufficient. No relative difficulty, truth probability, or independent formal verification follows from their position in the table.

Counterexamples to proposed deductions

The next constructions produce rational series from coefficients satisfying selected totient data. Others test a proposed estimate without changing the coefficients. We specify the retained assumptions in each case, so that the failed deduction can be distinguished from an argument using additional properties of φ\varphi. None decides the irrationality of SS.

Changing the coefficients after a finite prefix

Proposed argument. The quantified residue condition requires certificates beyond every starting index. A finite computation can check many instances, but one fixed inspection bound cannot establish these quantifiers. The following comparison explains this limitation without making any claim about all possible irrationality arguments. Erdos249257.TotientTailPeriodKiller.irrational_totient_series_iff_certificate_supply

Counterexample. Theorem 2.4 gives an explicit splice construction; its series value, exact reduced denominator and failure of the separation condition are checked in Lean. Choose an integer P>BP>B, set γ(n)=φ(n)\gamma(n)=\varphi(n) for n≤Bn\le B, and γ(n)=n−𝟏P∣n\gamma(n)=n-\mathbf 1_{P\mid n} for n>Bn>B. Then 0≤γ(n)≤n0\le\gamma(n)\le n, and the binary series ∑γ(n)/2n\sum\gamma(n)/2^n is rational: it is a finite rational prefix, plus the tail of ∑nn2−n\sum_n n2^{-n}, minus a geometric sum over the multiples of PP beyond BB. Because γ\gamma agrees with φ\varphi on every index ≤B\le B, γ\gamma passes every finite certificate that only inspects indices ≤B\le B; in particular it passes or fails every instance of 𝒞(h,N,L)\mathcal{C}(h,N,L) with N+h+L≤BN+h+L\le B exactly as φ\varphi does. Yet ∑γ(n)/2n∈ℚ\sum\gamma(n)/2^n\in\mathbb Q by construction.

Scope. For each fixed bound BB, a different rational comparison sequence can agree with φ\varphi on all inspected coefficients. This rules out a deduction from that finite prefix alone. It does not rule out a proof that establishes the required instances for arbitrarily large BB with the correct quantifiers. Such a proof would no longer be a single finite inspection. The comparison also does not preserve multiplicativity or every other arithmetic property of φ\varphi.

Consequence. The finite-prefix example and the parity example below are distinct constructions. The former preserves a prescribed finite prefix; the latter preserves parity and has separated nonperiodic blocks. Each shows why its own list of assumptions is insufficient. The recorded finite diagonal examples remain useful individual certificates, but their number alone gives no assertion at arbitrarily large scales. A rational series with matching totient parity

Matching totient parity and the bound c(n)≤nc(n)\le n does not determine the rationality of a binary sum. The example below is bounded and aperiodic, yet its sum is rational. Its paired changes can be placed beyond any threshold with any prescribed minimum separation.

Construction. Start with the sequence 0,1,1,2,4,4,4,…0,1,1,2,4,4,4,\ldots. At each position m=2k+3m=2^{k+3}, k≥0k\ge0, replace the pair (4,4)(4,4) at m,m+1m,m+1 by (6,0)(6,0). Equivalently, c(n)={0,n=0,1,n=1,2,2,n=3,6,n=2k+3 for some k≥0,0,n=2k+3+1 for some k≥0,4,otherwise.c(n)= \begin{cases} 0,&n=0,\\ 1,&n=1,2,\\ 2,&n=3,\\ 6,&n=2^{k+3}\text{ for some }k\ge0,\\ 0,&n=2^{k+3}+1\text{ for some }k\ge0,\\ 4,&\text{otherwise}. \end{cases} Each replacement leaves the binary sum unchanged because 2⋅2−m−4⋅2−(m+1)=02\cdot2^{-m}-4\cdot2^{-(m+1)}=0. The increasingly large gaps between replacements prevent eventual periodicity. The strongest recorded result also quantifies their separation:

Proposition 10.1 (A rational series preserving totient parity and the stated separation properties). There exists c:ℕ→ℕc:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N such that: c(n)≤6c(n)\le6 for all nn; c(n)≤nc(n)\le n; c(n)≡φ(n)(mod⁡2)c(n)\equiv\varphi(n)\pmod2 for every nn; for every N,G,KN,G,K there are KK pairs of coefficients (6,0)(6,0) starting beyond NN, with starting positions separated by more than GG; and ∑nc(n)/2n=3/2\sum_n c(n)/2^n = 3/2.

Scope. The displayed bounds, parity agreement and aperiodicity, including the stated number and separation of the edits, are jointly compatible with a rational binary sum. They therefore do not imply irrationality. The sequence cc differs from φ\varphi: the example preserves its parity, not all its arithmetic properties. It excludes an argument using only the listed assumptions, not every strengthening of an aperiodicity condition or every use of totient coefficients.

Consequence. The paired edits have zero total contribution, since 2⋅2−m−4⋅2−(m+1)=02\cdot2^{-m}-4\cdot2^{-(m+1)}=0. Applied at the specified sparse positions of this particular base sequence, they preserve the rational sum and the required bounds while preventing eventual periodicity. This does not construct a rational series for every prescribed parity pattern, and it is not the finite-prefix construction of Theorem 2.4. A proposed criterion using only the assumptions of this example must fail; a criterion using further arithmetic information is not addressed.

The cost of clearing a rational denominator

Clearing a denominator changes the multiplier as well as the fraction. The example 4(5/12)=5/34(5/12)=5/3 illustrates the divisibility relation below for arbitrary reduced fractions; no totient identity is needed.

Lemma 10.2 (Complement divisibility after multiplication). Write x=a/bx=a/b in lowest terms, where a∈ℤa\in\mathbb{Z} and b≥1b\ge1. Let c∈ℤc\in\mathbb{Z} and let HH be a positive divisor of bb. If the reduced denominator of cxcx divides HH, then b/H∣c.b/H\mid c.

Indeed, the hypothesis makes Hcx=Hca/bHcx=Hca/b integral. Since gcd⁡(a,b)=1\gcd(a,b)=1, it follows that b∣Hcb\mid Hc, hence b/H∣cb/H\mid c. Writing c=(b/H)tc=(b/H)t also gives Hcx=taHcx=ta; this equality is also proved in Lean (Erdos249257.AdelicHeightObstruction.scalarLocalization_integer_eq_mul_num). If a>0a>0, r≥0r\ge0, n≥1n\ge1, 2r∣a2^r\mid a, and a/b<2/(2n−1)a/b<2/(2^n-1), then 2r(2n−1)≤a(2n−1)<2b.2^r(2^n-1)\le a(2^n-1)<2b. Signed moments and parity

A signed determinant can serve in rational approximation only with both a nonzero numerator and a small error. Here parity proves the first requirement for the particular finite signed sum.

Lemma 10.3 (Nonvanishing from a unique largest denominator exponent). Let II be a finite set, let ui∈ℤu_i\in\mathbb{Z} and ei∈ℕe_i\in\mathbb{N} for i∈Ii\in I, and suppose that m∈Im\in I satisfies ei<eme_i<e_m for every i≠mi\ne m. If umu_m is odd, then 2em∑i∈Iui2ei=∑i∈Iui2em−ei≡1(mod⁡2).2^{e_m}\sum_{i\in I}\frac{u_i}{2^{e_i}} =\sum_{i\in I}u_i2^{e_m-e_i}\equiv1\pmod2. In particular, the sum is nonzero.

Every term except umu_m is even, which proves the assertion. For example, 1/2−1/8=3/81/2-1/8=3/8 has odd cleared numerator. Uniqueness is necessary for this argument: two odd contributions with the same largest exponent can cancel.

Lean also proves a separate determinant expansion from the Leibniz formula (det_mul_rectangular) and defines the truncated signed moments ∑N=1YaN2−N(k+1)\sum_{N=1}^Y a_N2^{-N(k+1)} and their Hankel determinants (truncatedMoment, hankelDet). The parity lemma is not derived from that determinant identity. A determinant application must first identify a sum to which the parity hypotheses apply.

For the totient series, one would still need suitable configurations at arbitrarily large scales and a denominator-weighted error tending to zero. Nonvanishing alone provides neither. No such family is supplied by these two algebraic statements; compare the separate rank discussion in §10.8. In another base, the analogous argument would require divisibility by a prime factor of that base rather than an unchanged appeal to parity.

Column rescaling and cancellation

A nonzero determinant need not prevent one row from being constant. For example, (111−1)(100−1)=(1−111).\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix} =\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}. The first and last matrices have determinants −2-2 and 22, respectively; the second row of the resulting matrix is constant. This simple column rescaling matters when a determinant is proposed as evidence for cancellation in the first-harmonic sums.

Proposition 10.4 (A nonzero minor survives inverse-phase column weights). Let d≥1d\ge1 be an integer, let e0,…,ed−1e_0,\ldots,e_{d-1} be nonnegative integers, and let z0,…,zd−1z_0,\ldots,z_{d-1} be nonzero complex numbers. Write Pij=zjeiP_{ij}=z_j^{e_i}, and suppose ei0=1e_{i_0}=1 for some i0i_0. Multiplying column jj by Wj=zj−1W_j=z_j^{-1} gives (Pdiag⁡(W))i0j=1,det⁡(Pdiag⁡(W))=det⁡(P)∏j=0d−1zj−1.(P\operatorname{diag}(W))_{i_0j}=1,\qquad \det(P\operatorname{diag}(W))=\det(P)\prod_{j=0}^{d-1}z_j^{-1}. Thus a nonzero determinant remains nonzero while row i0i_0 becomes constant. If all |zj|=1|z_j|=1, its absolute value is also unchanged.

The entry formula and the determinant of a product prove the statement. If row-dependent weights are allowed, the choice Wij=zji/zjeiW_{ij}=z_j^i/z_j^{e_i} gives WijPij=zjiW_{ij}P_{ij}=z_j^i and makes row zero constant. It produces the ordinary Vandermonde matrix, which is nonsingular when the zjz_j are pairwise distinct (rowResidualMonomialMatrix_reconstructs_phasePowerMatrix, rowReconstruction_zero_row_one).

These are statements about complex matrices, not arithmetic properties of the totient sequence. In particular, determinant nonvanishing, even with unit-modulus weights, does not by itself exclude complete alignment in the indicated row. An application of the first-harmonic criterion (irrational_totient_series_of_first_harmonic_norm_gap) needs additional information that excludes such weights or controls the resulting weighted sum. The example does not require that information to take the form of an identity coupling different rows, and it does not rule out determinant arguments that use appropriate additional hypotheses.

Tail integrality on an LCM grid

The comparison. The diagonal condition (Erdos249257.TotientTailPeriodKiller.irrational_totient_series_iff_lcm_diagonal_certificate_supply) uses the pair (Ht,2Ht)(H_t,2H_t). Under rationality, the same fractional part occurs at every positive multiple of HtH_t once tt is sufficiently large. A finite set of these multiples therefore gives another possible place to test for a nonintegral difference. The criterion below does not assert a smaller successful depth than the diagonal test.

Eventual equality of fractional parts.

Proposition 10.5 (Tail integrality on an LCM grid). S∈ℚ⟹∃t1,∀t≥t1,∀q,m:ℕ,0<q⟹R(q⋅H(t)+m⋅H(t))−R(q⋅H(t))∈ℤS\in\mathbb Q \implies \exists t_1,\ \forall t\ge t_1,\ \forall q,m:\mathbb N,\ 0<q \implies {R}(q\cdot {H}(t)+m\cdot{H}(t)) - {R}(q\cdot{H}(t)) \in \mathbb Z.

Rationality makes the fractional parts of RkHtR_{kH_t} equal for all k≥1k\ge1 at each scale t≥t1t\ge t_1. The corresponding implication, Theorem 6.53, shows that a certificate 𝒞(mHt,qHt,L)\mathcal C(mH_t,qH_t,L) with q≥1q\ge1 at arbitrarily large tt implies S∉ℚS\notin\mathbb Q.

(b′') A finite test on the grid.

Proposition 10.6 (A finite-grid certificate gives a nonintegral pair). Let Q⊆ℕ>0Q\subseteq\mathbb N_{>0} be finite and nonempty. For each q∈Qq\in Q, put Aq=∑j=1Lφ(qH+j)2L−jA_q=\sum_{j=1}^{L}\varphi(qH+j)2^{L-j} and Bq=qH+L+2B_q=qH+L+2. Suppose Bq<2LB_q<2^L for every q∈Qq\in Q and ∀qi∈Q∃qj∈Q,Bqj<(Aqi−Aqj)mod⁡2L.\forall q_i\in Q\ \exists q_j\in Q,\qquad B_{q_j}<(A_{q_i}-A_{q_j})\operatorname{mod}2^L. Then RqjH−RqiH∉ℤR_{q_jH}-R_{q_iH}\notin\mathbb Z for some qi,qj∈Qq_i,q_j\in Q. The proof and a four-point example are given in Theorem 6.56.

Scope. Eventual integrality on the LCM grid is a necessary consequence of rationality, not a claim about the actual series made without that hypothesis. The finite-grid test uses the individual one-sided bounds Bq<2LB_q<2^L, rather than charging the larger radius to both ends of a pairwise interval. This compares modulus bounds, not binary depths. A finite nonempty set and every stated size inequality are needed; three or more points and pairwise compatibility are not.

Neither statement supplies the unbounded family required to decide #249. Exhibiting a nonintegral tail difference on the LCM grid at arbitrarily large tt would refute rationality. The finite-grid test is a way to certify such a difference, not a proof that these tests succeed at arbitrarily large scales.

The implication from rationality to grid flatness (rational_totient_series_forces_lcm_cone_flatness) should not be confused with an assertion of flatness for the actual series. The exact diagonal integrality reformulation and its quantified converse (diagonal_int_iff_foreignDiagonalDefect_hits_fullTarget, irrational_totientSeries_of_full_target_avoidance_supply) give other equivalent forms of the problem. They are not the only such forms; Proposition 1.8 lists further equivalent certificate conditions.

Consequence. Choosing the least deep tail is the step that turns a common-fractional-part assumption into an intersection of arcs. A related finite comparison concerns first and second differences: at (h,N)=(1,8)(h,N)=(1,8) the first-difference test holds at depth 88, while no second-difference certificate exists at depth at most 88 (totient_tail_rank_two_kill_sound_but_not_shallower_cell). This disproves a universal claim of smaller depth for second differences; it does not show that they can never improve a certificate.

Exact dyadic rank and the limits of a rank argument

The dyadic case gives an explicit basis for each finite level and for the union of all levels. Coons proved nonregularity in every base k≥2k\ge2 ; here the rank is computed at each finite level and the basis is given explicitly. Martin’s Theorem 1 supplies independence for the positive-residue affine forms [4], leaving the two zero-residue sections to be treated separately. The all-base independence proof and the integral relation proof are given separately in the short paper.

Construction.

Theorem 10.7 (Exact dyadic rank and infinite-dimensionality). For every e≥1e\ge1, the family {n↦φ(n),n↦φ(2n)}∪{n↦φ(2jn+r):1≤j≤e,0<r<2j,r odd}\{n\mapsto\varphi(n),\ n\mapsto\varphi(2n)\} \ \cup\ \{n\mapsto\varphi(2^j n+r):1\le j\le e,\ 0<r<2^j,\ r\text{ odd}\} is linearly independent over ℚ\mathbb{Q}. It contains 2e+12^e+1 sequences and spans the sections through level ee by the zero- and even-residue reductions.

The two zero-residue sections need separate treatment because their arguments nn and 2n2n are proportional. Restrict a proposed relation to n=2m+1n=2m+1, where φ(2n)=φ(n)\varphi(2n)=\varphi(n). The odd-residue sections, together with φ(n)\varphi(n), now have pairwise nonproportional affine arguments. The evaluation-matrix construction chooses one input per row. At that input a selected primitive form is prime, while each competing form has a prime divisor whose predecessor is divisible by a fixed auxiliary prime. The matrix is diagonal and nonzero on the diagonal modulo that auxiliary prime. The check that the selected prime progression is reduced is part of the construction.

Independence removes the positive-residue coefficients and leaves A+B=0A+B=0. The same remaining relation at n=2n=2 gives A+2B=0A+2B=0, so both coefficients vanish. This is the dyadic specialisation of the short paper’s proof. The Lean proof is unconditional; it uses the Chinese remainder theorem and Dirichlet’s theorem on primes in arithmetic progressions from Mathlib. Consequently the full infinite family spans an infinite-dimensional ℚ\mathbb Q-space (not_finiteDimensional_span_fullTotientKernel). A separate elementary observation concerns a proposed integer identity. There are no Q,v∈ℕ>0Q,v\in\mathbb{N}_{>0} and A,b∈ℤA,b\in\mathbb{Z} with QvA=bQvA=b, A≠0A\ne0, and |b|<Qv|b|<Qv: the identity forces |b|=Qv|A|≥Qv|b|=Qv|A|\ge Qv (false_of_compressedAdjointCertificate).

The Lean independence theorem is also stated for e=0e=0, but its auxiliary canonical index then still contains the two zero-residue sections φ(n)\varphi(n) and φ(2n)\varphi(2n). It is therefore not the actual truncation through level zero, which consists only of φ(n)\varphi(n) and has dimension one.

Integral relations.

The independence statement also determines the arithmetic of the section lattice. Fix e≥1e\ge1, write Fj,r(n)=φ(2jn+r)F_{j,r}(n)=\varphi(2^j n+r), and let Ie={(j,r):0≤j≤e,0≤r<2j}I_e=\{(j,r):0\le j\le e,\ 0\le r<2^j\}. Retain F0,0F_{0,0}, F1,0F_{1,0}, and the odd-residue sections at levels 1,…,e1,\ldots,e; call this retained index set JeJ_e. The totient identities reduce every omitted section to Fi=aiFj(i)F_i=a_iF_{j(i)} for a retained section j(i)j(i) and an integer ai≥0a_i\ge0. Thus the retained family generates the lattice Le=∑i∈IeℤFiL_e=\sum_{i\in I_e}\mathbb Z F_i. Its rational independence gives integer independence as well: every element of LeL_e has unique integer coordinates in these 2e+12^e+1 retained sections.

To describe all integral relations, let EiE_i denote the formal coordinate vector in ℤIe\mathbb Z^{I_e} and use the evaluation map $$\adjustbox{max width=\linewidth}{$\displaystyle \operatorname{ev}_e:\mathbb Z^{I_e}\longrightarrow L_e, \qquad (c_i)\longmapsto\sum_{i\in I_e}c_iF_i. $}$$ For each omitted index put Ri=Ei−aiEj(i)R_i=E_i-a_iE_{j(i)}. Then $$\adjustbox{max width=\linewidth}{$\displaystyle \ker(\operatorname{ev}_e) =\bigoplus_{i\in I_e\mathbin{\backslash} J_e}\mathbb Z R_i, \qquad \operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb Z}\ker(\operatorname{ev}_e)=2^e-2. $}$$ Indeed, subtracting ∑i∉JeciRi\sum_{i\notin J_e}c_iR_i removes all omitted coordinates. At a retained index jj, the remaining coefficient is cj+∑i∉Je,j(i)=jaicic_j+\sum_{i\notin J_e,\,j(i)=j}a_i c_i. These are the integral coordinates of the original combination. If it is a relation, independence makes every one of them zero. Conversely, the coefficient of EiE_i in ∑h∉JebhRh\sum_{h\notin J_e}b_hR_h is exactly bib_i, proving uniqueness. Each relation row has coefficient 11 in its own omitted coordinate and 00 in every other omitted coordinate. No division is needed, so the conclusion holds over ℤ\mathbb{Z}. The depth-two base-six example in the short paper illustrates these two-term rows. The distinction between the retained basis and the redundant spanning family of all sections already matters for kk-regular sequences that are not eventually zero: their growth exponent is the base-kk logarithm of the joint spectral radius of their section matrices in a basis, whereas a redundant spanning family gives only an upper bound (Coons [3]). The totient is not regular, so that theorem does not apply; the short paper records how the section maps act on the retained bases from one level to the next.

The integral normal form and the full dyadic rational basis are formally checked in Lean. The formal statement gives the same construction for every integer base k≥2k\ge2, with relation rank ∑j=1e−1kj\sum_{j=1}^{e-1}k^j. The full dyadic assembly separately gives a basis for the infinite rational span and for its finitely supported rational relations. These finite and infinite statements should not be confused with a claim about infinite sums of relations.

Relation to the series value. Infinite section rank does not imply irrationality of SS. The result quantifies the nonregularity already cited above: it gives the rank, the retained sections and their integral relations. Martin’s simultaneous inequalities supply another proof for pairwise nonproportional affine forms with positive slopes [4]. His theorem does not separate nn from 2n2n; the two evaluations above do that. The linked Lean proof is independent of Martin’s theorem.

The same independence argument also bounds the rank of an integral carry. If S∈ℚS\in\mathbb{Q}, choose an integer v>0v>0 with vS∈ℤvS\in\mathbb{Z} and put uN=vRNu_N=vR_N, where RN=∑j≥1φ(N+j)2−jR_N=\sum_{j\ge1}\varphi(N+j)2^{-j}. Then uN∈ℤu_N\in\mathbb{Z}, uN+1=2uN−vφ(N+1),0≤uN≤v(N+2),uN/2N→0.u_{N+1}=2u_N-v\varphi(N+1),\qquad 0\le u_N\le v(N+2),\qquad u_N/2^N\longrightarrow0. For every e≥0e\ge0, dim⁡ℚspan⁡{n↦u2jn+r:1≤j≤e,0≤r<2j}≥2e−1.\dim_{\mathbb{Q}}\operatorname{span} \{n\mapsto u_{2^j n+r}:1\le j\le e,\ 0\le r<2^j\} \ \ge\ 2^e-1. This is the finite family in the linked statement (not_irrational_totientSeries_implies_unbounded_carryRank_unconditional); it contains all carry residues at levels 1,…,e1,\ldots,e, not just odd residues or an unspecified retained subfamily. Indeed, for each odd rr with 0<r<2j0<r<2^j, the recurrence gives vφ(2jn+r)=2u2jn+r−1−u2jn+r.v\varphi(2^j n+r)=2u_{2^j n+r-1}-u_{2^j n+r}. These 2e−12^e-1 totient sections are independent and belong to the span of the displayed carry sections after multiplication by v≠0v\ne0. The rank bound follows. The boundary condition uN/2N→0u_N/2^N\to0 identifies the canonical carry, but is not used in this rank-transfer argument.

To contradict rationality by rank, one would also need an incompatible upper bound. The comparison series with value 5/45/4 in Section 12.6 shows why rationality, a binary carry recurrence and linear coefficient growth alone do not supply such a bound. Its coefficients agree with φ\varphi at odd indices but differ at even indices; they are not the totient sequence. Thus this comparison does not exclude an argument using additional totient identities.

A separate finite-dimensional calculation concerns the matrix UN(i,j)=μ((i+1)/(j+1))U_N(i,j)=\mu((i+1)/(j+1)) when (j+1)∣(i+1)(j+1)\mid(i+1) and zero otherwise, for 0≤i,j<N0\le i,j<N. It is lower triangular with diagonal entries one. Hence det⁡UN=1\det U_N=1 and the map x↦UNxx\mapsto U_Nx is injective (incidenceMobius_det_eq_one). This proves injectivity of that particular map, not the impossibility of every finite-dimensional argument for irrationality.

The evaluation-matrix argument. For functions f1,…,fsf_1,\ldots,f_s with values in a field, points n1,…,nsn_1,\ldots,n_s for which det⁡(fj(ni))≠0\det(f_j(n_i))\ne0 prove linear independence: evaluating a relation gives an invertible linear system for its coefficients. This elementary criterion is Proposition 6.24. It does not, by itself, construct the points. Here the totient formula, CRT and Dirichlet’s theorem provide them for nonproportional affine forms, followed by the separate zero-residue argument. Another arithmetic function would require its own argument for nonvanishing of the evaluation determinant.

Signed interpolation with entire Dirichlet defects

To vary a series value while preserving every fixed moment condition, we use disjoint finite differences of increasing order. Their orders make the later differences invisible to each fixed moment, while overlapping integer ranges for their amplitudes fill an interval of values at a reciprocal integer base. The construction below leaves every odd totient coefficient fixed and preserves Dirichlet singularities on every fixed arithmetic progression. The three numbered remarks in this subsection have ordinary proofs; their formalisation in Lean remains outstanding.

The change of sign is indispensable for this construction. An infinitely supported nonnegative integer correction has unbounded Abel limit at one. The Dirichlet series of the correction also cannot extend to an entire function if its defining series converges in a right half-plane. Indeed, choose a positive real σ\sigma inside that half-plane. Termwise differentiation gives (−1)kD(k)(σ)=∑ne(n)n−σ(log⁡n)k≥0(-1)^kD^{(k)}(\sigma)=\sum_ne(n)n^{-\sigma}(\log n)^k\ge0. Integer nonnegativity forces finite support, and a finite correction at an integer reciprocal base cannot change rationality. Signed differences are what allow the stronger observation class above.

Hypotheses of the conditional implications

Uniformity in a parameter does not remove a hypothesis. An implication can hold at every scale although the required arithmetic input is known at only finitely many scales, or at none. We examine that distinction for the displayed implications, without drawing conclusions about all arguments that use the same objects.

Implications concerning the totient series

Cancellation versus a certificate.

The first-harmonic implication converts the stated cosine bound on one block into a finite residue certificate (exists_certifiedKill_of_first_harmonic_gap). To prove irrationality, the bound must hold with the quantifiers in Section 3: for every shift and beyond every block threshold. A finite identity for the sum, or a computation at one block, does not establish this assertion.

Sign versus distance from an integer.

The positivity theorem for the LCM tail difference (actualLcmTailDiff_shift_pos) identifies the relevant endpoint under the stated size and modulus bounds. Nonintegrality follows only after excluding the corresponding residue interval (actualLcmTailDiff_notMem_int_of_topEdgeResidueGap). Likewise, the terminal-dominance condition is a sufficient hypothesis, not a construction of the required parameters (PowerTwoFlexibleActualTerminalDominanceSupply). Under integrality its inequality contradicts positivity of the terminal carry; the contradiction establishes sufficiency, not the inequality itself.

An error bound versus a separated approximation.

The finite-tail approximation has a uniform error radius (abs_actualLcmTailOrbit_sub_rawApprox_lt). The cited exact check supplies nonintegrality at the two exponents a=4,6a=4,6 (actualLcmTailOrbit_four_and_six_notMem_int); it is not an assertion that no other exponent works. To obtain irrationality by this criterion, separation must occur at arbitrarily large LCM scales. In the nondivisor approximation of Section 6.6.8, the error bound is also proved when D≥2HD\ge2H. Its remaining requirement is finite rational separation, not an additional convergence hypothesis.

Denominator growth versus approximation quality.

The lower bound for the product of the upper-half Mersenne factors (upperHalfMersenneProduct_lower_bound) concerns a denominator expression. An irrationality argument needs a comparison with the error of the corresponding approximation. Growth of that denominator expression alone does not give either a successful residue test or a nonintegral totient tail.

A rank lower bound versus a contradiction.

The coefficient independence and hypothetical-carry rank bounds hold uniformly in the level (linearIndependent_canonicalTotientKernelFamily, not_irrational_totientSeries_implies_unbounded_carryRank_unconditional). A contradiction would require an upper bound for the actual carry that is strictly smaller than the lower bound at some level. The rational 5/45/4 comparison disproves the proposed generic upper bound. The separate integer boundary conditions in the cited adjugate calculation are inconsistent (false_of_compressedAdjointCertificate), but that calculation does not exclude matrix arguments with different boundary conditions.

Related source comparisons for Problem #257

The following comparisons concern Problem #257 and are included with the hypotheses of their cited sources. No statement in this subsection is an input to a proof about SS.

The comparison of the middle-carry estimate (one_third_lt_scaledMersenneTail_floorWall) with the remainder estimate (SeamGreedyRemainderGapBound) distinguishes the direction of an inequality from control of the required deviation. No unconditional proof of the associated sign claim is supplied, and a sign alone would not give a lower bound for the magnitude.

The row-capacity and later-skip implications retain their respective local deficit and skip hypotheses (exists_exactRowStrictUpperFill_of_skippedCoreSharpCapacity, halfGreedy_precriticalSuffix_lt_of_future_skip_after_takenBlock). The finite-shadow comparison distinguished an existential horizon, obtained from convergence, from the particular horizon J=k−2J=k-2 needed in that application (exists_greedyHalfFrozenMargin_nonneg_of_excess_neg). The terminal-strip formulation also imposes its own support and carry restrictions (HalfCarryCofinalTerminalOnlyStrip); a bound on carry size does not automatically replace a restriction on the positions of the nonzero coefficients.

For finite sums of 1/(2n−1)1/(2^n-1), the common denominator is odd. Their reduced denominators are therefore odd, so they cannot equal a rational number with even reduced denominator. This is the elementary reason behind the finite-support exclusion and its denominator source (finite_boolSupport_ne_half, finiteErdosSum_den_odd). The cited infinite-skipping theorem is stated for the target 1/21/2 (infinite_greedyMersenneSkippedSupport_of_half_mem). A proposed extension to other targets requires checking that theorem’s hypotheses and proof; the finite-denominator observation alone does not prove such an extension or the needed infinite-orbit estimate.

Finally, the support-fraction statement and the more general collision bound have distinct hypotheses (dyadic_support_fraction_reciprocalMass_diverges_or_gt_one, shiftedBooleanCollision_wrap_bound_of_common_multiple). A broader use would need an additional mean-residue estimate, which is not supplied, and the endpoint proofs of the dichotomy in the linked Lean source have not been checked for a changed target (half_mem_mersenneAchievementSet_or_exists_fatal_gap). No such extension is used here.

Quantifiers must be checked independently.

For example, a statement of the form ∃N∃L∀h\exists N\,\exists L\,\forall h does not provide the required ∀h∀N0∃N≥N0∃L\forall h\,\forall N_0\,\exists N\ge N_0\,\exists L. The first assertion controls many shifts at one location; the second requires arbitrarily late locations for each fixed shift. Relabelling a source statement does not bridge this difference.

Additional mathematics required by the sufficient conditions

We turn from the proved reductions to the estimates needed to apply them. The doubling identity relates window phases to exact tails; the subsequent decompositions separate the weighted sums for which cancellation is required. The suggested analytic applications remain proposals where those estimates are missing. Failure of one application does not exclude the analytic method.

The section contains a doubling-orbit formulation with explicit thresholds, a lacunary comparison sequence for the strength of a block estimate, and sufficient estimates for the prime-factor decomposition. The discussion of a rank upper bound must also be read with the rational 5/45/4 comparison sequence: rationality alone does not give bounded rank. These are the scope distinctions needed to interpret the individual statements, not priority claims.

The proved reductions identify explicit sufficient hypotheses. Those hypotheses remain to be established; the reductions do not prove them.

The doubling identity

Write S=∑n≥1φ(n)/2nS=\sum_{n\ge 1}\varphi(n)/2^n, RN=∑m≥1φ(N+m)/2mR_N=\sum_{m\ge 1}\varphi(N+m)/2^m for the local tail (Erdos249257.TotientTailPeriodKiller.totientTail), and ΦN=∑n≤Nφ(n)2N−n∈ℤ\Phi_N=\sum_{n\le N}\varphi(n)2^{N-n}\in\mathbb{Z} for the integer prefix, so that 2NS=ΦN+RN2^N S=\Phi_N+R_N. For h≥1h\ge 1 set αh:=(2h−1)S.\alpha_h \;:=\; (2^h-1)\,S .

Lemma 12.1 (The doubling identity). For all N≥0N\ge 0 and h≥1h\ge 1, RN+1=2RN−φ(N+1),RN+h−RN=2Nαh−(ΦN+h−ΦN),R_{N+1}=2R_N-\varphi(N+1), \qquad R_{N+h}-R_N \;=\; 2^N\alpha_h-\bigl(\Phi_{N+h}-\Phi_N\bigr), so RN+h−RN≡2Nαh(mod⁡1)R_{N+h}-R_N \equiv 2^N\alpha_h \pmod 1, and consequently the exact first character of the tail difference is the ×2\times 2 orbit of one real number: e(RN+h−RN)=e(2Nαh),e(x):=exp⁡(2πix).e(R_{N+h}-R_N) \;=\; e\bigl(2^N\alpha_h\bigr), \qquad e(x):=\exp(2\pi i x). Hence, for fixed hh, the phases {RN+h−RNmod⁡1}N≥0\{\,R_{N+h}-R_N \operatorname{mod} 1\,\}_{N\ge 0} are the forward orbit of αhmod⁡1\alpha_h \operatorname{mod} 1 under x↦2xx\mapsto 2x.

The recurrence RN+1=2RN−φ(N+1)R_{N+1}=2R_N-\varphi(N+1) is one line from the definition and is used below only for intuition.

These identities express the phases as a lacunary exponential sum in one real variable. The next proposition transfers an estimate for that orbit to the truncated phases, accounting for the truncation error. The identities themselves are already in the cited sources.

Proposition 12.2 (Transfer to the doubling orbit). Suppose that ∀h≥1∀X0∃X≥max⁡(X0,1):∑N=X2X−1cos⁡(2π2Nαh)≤89100X.\forall h\ge 1\ \forall X_0\ \exists X\ge \max(X_0,1):\quad \sum_{N=X}^{2X-1}\cos\bigl(2\pi\,2^{N}\alpha_h\bigr)\;\le\;\tfrac{89}{100}\,X . This hypothesis implies that SS is irrational.

Proof. Fix h≥1h\ge 1 and X0X_0, and take XX as supplied. Choose L≥hL\ge h with 2L≥1024(2X+h+L+2)2^{L}\ge 1024\,(2X+h+L+2); such LL exists because 2L/L→∞2^L/L\to\infty, and it satisfies the size inequality 16(2X+h+L+2)≤2L16(2X+h+L+2)\le 2^L a fortiori. The proof above makes the truncation margin explicit. The full implication is also proved in Lean (ErdosProblems.Erdos249.irrational_totient_series_of_tailOrbitBlockGap). It uses a real-part estimate for the exact phases and spends 1/1001/100 on truncation. Compare the sufficient norm condition of Theorem 6.59. This is a separately sufficient condition. It is not asserted to be equivalent to the 21/2521/25 norm bound or to the four separate estimates stated above. The constants account for different quantities and different error margins.

Corollary 12.3 (A digit version of the analytic condition). Let ρh(X)\rho_h(X) denote the proportion of N∈[X,2X)N\in[X,2X) with ∥2Nαh∥ℝ/ℤ≥1/4\|2^N\alpha_h\|_{\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}}\ge 1/4. If for every h≥1h\ge 1 there are cofinally many XX with ρh(X)≥11/100\rho_h(X)\ge 11/100, then SS is irrational. For nondyadic αh\alpha_h, the condition counted by ρh(X)\rho_h(X) is exactly a change between binary digits N+1N+1 and N+2N+2. Thus the same sufficient hypothesis asks for at least 11X/10011X/100 such changes, counted with X≤N<2XX\le N<2X, on arbitrarily large blocks for every hh.

Proof. The inequality ∥x∥ℝ/ℤ≥1/4\|x\|_{\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}}\ge1/4 gives cos⁡(2πx)≤0\cos(2\pi x)\le0. Every remaining term is at most 11, so ∑N=X2X−1cos⁡(2π2Nαh)≤(1−ρh(X))X≤89100X.\sum_{N=X}^{2X-1}\cos(2\pi 2^N\alpha_h) \le(1-\rho_h(X))X\le\frac{89}{100}X. Proposition 12.2 now applies. For the digit reading, for a nondyadic αh\alpha_h the fractional part of 2Nαh2^N\alpha_h is in [1/4,3/4][1/4,3/4] exactly when those two binary digits differ. The nondyadic qualification excludes the endpoint ambiguity at 3/43/4. ◻

The exact hypothesis is the digit-change inequality in the corollary. It is not a claim about an average run length: the two boundary runs of a finite block need not be complete, and their lengths are not specified by the number of interior digit changes. The finite observations below satisfy the displayed bound at their sampled parameters. They do not establish it on arbitrarily large blocks.

Observation 12.4. Lemma 12.1 expresses each tail phase in terms of the doubling orbit of αh=(2h−1)S\alpha_h=(2^h-1)S. The block conditions average those phases, the prime condition samples prescribed prime-indexed positions, and the full-depth condition requires a finite residue certificate for each (d,N)(d,N) at some multiple of dd. Corollary 12.3 gives one sufficient digit-change test for the real-part estimate; it is not an equivalence with the norm bound or with the four separate budgets. Likewise, a bound on a binary run length is not the exact prime-gap condition. Section 12.7 compares the original inequalities.

The full-block exponential-sum estimate

The required inequality.

∀h≥1∀X0∃X,L:max⁡(X0,1)≤X,16(2X+h+L+2)≤2L,∥∑N=X2X−1e(D(h,N,L)/2L)∥≤2125X,\forall h\ge 1\ \forall X_0\ \exists X,L:\quad \max(X_0,1)\le X,\quad 16(2X+h+L+2)\le 2^{L},\quad \Bigl\|\sum_{N=X}^{2X-1} e\bigl(D(h,N,L)/2^{L}\bigr)\Bigr\|\le \tfrac{21}{25}X, where D(h,N,L)=∑j<L(φ(N+h+1+j)−φ(N+1+j))2L−1−jD(h,N,L)=\sum_{j<L}\bigl(\varphi(N+h+1+j)-\varphi(N+1+j)\bigr)2^{L-1-j}. This inequality is unproved; it implies irrationality (Erdos249257.TotientTailPeriodKiller.DTWFirstHarmonicNormGap, Erdos249257.irrational_totient_series_of_first_harmonic_norm_gap). By Proposition 12.2 the real-part bound with constant 89/10089/100 for the exact doubling phases suffices; its transfer to the truncated phases uses the separate error estimate in that proposition.

The discrepancy in terms of the doubling map.

For L≥hL\ge h, dividing by 2L2^L and reindexing the two ranges gives D(h,N,L)2L=−∑t=1hφ(N+t)2t⏟head+(2h−1)∑t=h+1Lφ(N+t)2t⏟body+∑t=L+1L+hφ(N+t)2t−h⏟tail.\begin{equation} \label{eq:window} \frac{D(h,N,L)}{2^{L}} =\underbrace{-\sum_{t=1}^{h}\frac{\varphi(N+t)}{2^{t}}}_{\text{head}} \;+\;\underbrace{(2^{h}-1)\sum_{t=h+1}^{L}\frac{\varphi(N+t)}{2^{t}}}_{\text{body}} \;+\;\underbrace{\sum_{t=L+1}^{L+h}\frac{\varphi(N+t)}{2^{t-h}}}_{\text{tail}} . \end{equation}

The phase is a geometrically weighted sum of totients at L+hL+h consecutive arguments. In the first two ranges, 1≤t≤L1\le t\le L, the coefficient has denominator 2t2^t and odd numerator. Its contribution is therefore integral exactly when v2(φ(N+t))≥tv_2(\varphi(N+t))\ge t. In the last range, L<t≤L+hL<t\le L+h, the denominator is instead 2t−h2^{t-h}, so the corresponding threshold is t−ht-h. Here v2(a)v_2(a) denotes the exponent of 22 in the positive integer aa. The selected offset in the four-term decomposition lies in the middle range, where the odd multiplier is 2h−12^h-1.

Relevant comparison estimates.

The following comparisons identify the estimates still needed; they do not rule out these methods.

Weyl differencing and van der Corput. The van der Corput inequality applies to arbitrary bounded complex sequences , but its use here requires estimates for shifted correlations. For the exact phases xN=2Nαhx_N=2^N\alpha_h of Lemma 12.1, xN+q−xN=(2q−1)xN.x_{N+q}-x_N=(2^q-1)x_N. Thus differencing gives another doubling orbit, not a polynomial phase of lower degree. The finite phase D(h,N,L)/2LD(h,N,L)/2^L approximates this orbit modulo 11; it is not the exact orbit itself. No bound for the resulting correlations is established here.

The large sieve. A proposed application would need a suitable family of separated frequencies and a way to recover a bound for each fixed hh. Averaging only over hh would not suffice: the condition asks for a block estimate for every hh, not for most of them.

Bilinear sums over prime factors. Factoring N+t=mpN+t=mp and using φ(mp)=φ(m)(p−1)\varphi(mp)=\varphi(m)(p-1) makes the selected totient contribution linear in the prime pp. Section 12.3 gives this decomposition and identifies the remaining weight. A bound for that weight is still needed before a Vaughan- or Vinogradov-type argument can be applied.

Erdős’s 1948 digit method. The comparison series is E=∑n≥11/(2n−1)=∑N≥1d(N)/2NE=\sum_{n\ge1}1/(2^n-1)=\sum_{N\ge1}d(N)/2^N, whose irrationality Erdős proved [11]. For the totient series, the corresponding Möbius expansion is exact: φ=μ*id\varphi=\mu * \mathrm{id} gives S=∑d≥1μ(d)2d(2d−1)2\begin{equation} \label{eq:mobmers} S=\sum_{d\ge 1}\mu(d)\,\frac{2^{d}}{(2^{d}-1)^{2}} \end{equation} The identity follows by Möbius inversion; a numerical computation gives S=1.3676308019850223…S=1.3676308019850223\ldots to sixteen digits.

Erdős combines congruences forcing increasing powers of 22 to divide a block of divisor counts with an averaged tail bound, producing long zero blocks in the binary expansion . To adapt that argument here, one would need congruences for the actual totient coefficients together with a compatible tail estimate. The identities alone provide neither combination. In [eq:mobmers], the coefficients μ(d)\mu(d) can have either sign, so positivity of the original totient series does not give positivity term by term in this expansion. This is a limitation of the proposed direct transfer, not a proof that a digit argument or a different use of the Möbius expansion cannot work.

The unresolved estimate.

For general coefficients 0≤c(n)≤n0\le c(n)\le n, irrationality alone does not imply the block norm condition. The following example has very sparse nonzero coefficients. It is irrational, but almost all phases in each sufficiently large block lie close to 11.

Theorem 12.5 (The block norm condition is stronger in the class 0≤c(n)≤n0\le c(n)\le n). Let c(n)=1c(n)=1 if n=k!n=k! for some k≥1k\ge 1 and c(n)=0c(n)=0 otherwise, so 0≤c(n)≤n0\le c(n)\le n for all n≥1n\ge 1, and let β=∑n≥1c(n)/2n=∑k≥12−k!\beta=\sum_{n\ge1}c(n)/2^{n} =\sum_{k\ge 1}2^{-k!}. Then β\beta is irrational, and for every h≥1h\ge 1 and every X≥81(h+5)X\ge 81(h+5), ∑N=X2X−1cos⁡(2π2N(2h−1)β)>910X.\sum_{N=X}^{2X-1}\cos\bigl(2\pi\,2^{N}(2^{h}-1)\beta\bigr) \;>\; \tfrac{9}{10}X . Consequently the block norm condition fails for β\beta at every sufficiently large scale, for every admissible truncation depth, even though β\beta is irrational. Thus irrationality, nonnegative integer coefficients and the bound c(n)≤nc(n)\le n do not imply the block gap. A proof for SS needs an additional property not shared by this example; the comparison does not specify which additional property will suffice.

Proof. The binary expansion of β\beta has infinitely many ones separated by unbounded strings of zeros. It is not eventually periodic, so β\beta is irrational. Write γ=(2h−1)β\gamma=(2^h-1)\beta, and let k!k! be the least factorial greater than NN. The earlier terms become integers after multiplication by 2N2^N, so 2Nγ≡(2h−1)∑j≥k2N−j!(mod⁡ℤ).2^N\gamma\equiv(2^h-1)\sum_{j\ge k}2^{N-j!}\pmod{\mathbb Z}. If N≤k!−h−5N\le k!-h-5, the expression on the right lies between 00 and 2⋅2N+h−k!≤1/162\cdot2^{N+h-k!}\le1/16. Thus ∥2Nγ∥ℝ/ℤ≤1/16\|2^N\gamma\|_{\mathbb R/\mathbb Z}\le1/16 and cos⁡(2π2Nγ)≥cos⁡(π/8)>9238/10000\cos(2\pi 2^{N}\gamma)\ge\cos(\pi/8)>9238/10000. The remaining NN lie in (k!−h−5,k!](k!-h-5,\,k!], at most h+5h+5 values per factorial. The relevant factorials have ratio at least 33, and h+5<Xh+5<X, so [X,2X)[X,2X) meets at most one such interval. Hence the sum is greater than 923810000(X−h−5)−(h+5)≥910X+h+5250\frac{9238}{10000}(X-h-5)-(h+5)\ge\frac9{10}X+\frac{h+5}{250} when X≥81(h+5)X\ge81(h+5).

To pass from these exact phases to the finite residue test, note that 0≤c(n)≤10\le c(n)\le1 puts each scaled tail in [0,1][0,1]. The error in the truncated tail difference is therefore at most 2−L2^{-L}, so each complex phase changes by at most 2π2−L2\pi2^{-L}. At an admissible depth, 2L≥16(2X+h+L+2)>32X2^L\ge16(2X+h+L+2)>32X, and the total change in the block sum is less than π/16\pi/16. Its real part is consequently greater than 9X/10−π/16>21X/259X/10-\pi/16>21X/25 for X≥81(h+5)X\ge81(h+5). Its norm cannot satisfy the 21X/2521X/25 bound either. ◻

This example rules out the implication from irrationality and the stated coefficient bound to the block norm condition. It does not say that the totient sum is Liouville-like, or that every argument based on its digits fails. A proof of the block estimate must use information that distinguishes the actual totient phases from this comparison sequence.

The size of the required saving.

Under Lebesgue measure on the phase circle, the binary digit maps are independent fair bits. The digit-change proportion therefore tends to 1/21/2 for almost every phase. For almost every phase, the real-part block sum is also O(Xlog⁡log⁡X)O(\sqrt{X\log\log X}), by the law of the iterated logarithm of Erdős and Gál for lacunary series [29]. The block bound follows by subtracting two initial partial sums. An almost-everywhere theorem supplies no conclusion at the particular phase αh=(2h−1)S\alpha_h=(2^h-1)S. The requirement is ρh≥0.11\rho_h\ge 0.11 and a saving of a constant factor. The finite values in Table [tab:blocks] have ρh\rho_h near 0.500.50 and small block averages. They are compatible with square-root cancellation, but do not establish its asymptotic order. The sufficient condition asks only for the stated fixed saving on arbitrarily large blocks. No estimate in this record supplies it for the totient phases.

The four-term decomposition

The simultaneous inequalities.

Use the four finite sums defined in Section 3.2; in particular, each group mean averages the selected prime phase, not the residual weight. For every h≥1h\ge 1 there must exist s≥1s\ge 1 and η∈(0,1)\eta\in(0,1) such that for every X0X_0 there are X≥max⁡(X0,1)X\ge\max(X_0,1) and LL with h≤L−sh\le L-s, 16(2X+h+L+2)≤2L16(2X+h+L+2)\le 2^{L}, and all four of Re⁡∑N∈𝒢wN(zN−z‾mN)≤1425X,∥∑N∈𝒢wNz‾mN∥≤1100X,∥∑N∈𝒜∖𝒢E(h,N,L)∥≤1100X,∥∑X≤N<2XmathbbN∉𝒜E(h,N,L)∥≤825X.\begin{aligned} \operatorname{Re}\sum_{N\in\mathcal G}w_N(z_N-\bar z_{m_N}) &\le\tfrac{14}{25}X,\\ \left\lVert\sum_{N\in\mathcal G}w_N\bar z_{m_N}\right\rVert &\le\tfrac{1}{100}X,\\ \left\lVert\sum_{N\in\mathcal A\smallsetminus\mathcal G}E(h,N,L)\right\rVert &\le\tfrac{1}{100}X,\\ \left\lVert\sum_{\substack{X\le N<2X\\mathbb{N}\notin\mathcal A}}E(h,N,L)\right\rVert &\le\tfrac{8}{25}X. \end{aligned} These inequalities are unproved; together they imply irrationality (Erdos249257.TotientTailPeriodKiller.DTWPivotResidualDecorrelation, Erdos249257.irrational_totient_series_of_pivotResidualDecorrelation). The decomposition is an exact identity (Erdos249257.TotientTailPeriodKiller.windowFirstExp_sum_eq_pivot_decomposition). It separates two different tasks. The last two sums can be bounded by counting their indices, since every phase has modulus one. The first two retain the weight wNw_N: subtracting the group mean does not remove its correlation with the selected prime phase. The parameters s,ηs,\eta must be fixed before X0X_0, and the estimates must hold for the same X,LX,L; separate successful blocks do not suffice. For X≥4X\ge4 and s=L−hs=L-h, the single cofactor group mN=1m_N=1, not the full assigned set, consists of the indices for which N+h+1N+h+1 is prime (Erdos249257.TotientTailPeriodKiller.mem_pivotFiber_one_overlap_iff).

An upper bound for the unassigned terms.

An unassigned index has a smooth shifted argument, but the converse is not asserted. The factorisation gives the containment needed for an upper bound on the number of unassigned indices.

Proposition 12.6 (A one-sided bound for the unassigned terms). Fix h,sh,s and choose the admissible depth LL minimally for each large XX. Put t=L−s+1=Oh,s(log⁡X)t=L-s+1=O_{h,s}(\log X) and yX=4X+2t/Xy_X=4\sqrt X+2t/\sqrt X. If n=N+tn=N+t is unassigned, then its largest prime factor satisfies P(n)≤yXP(n)\le y_X. Consequently #{N∈[X,2X):N∉𝒜}≤Ψ(2X+t−1,yX)−Ψ(X+t−1,yX)=(1−log⁡2+o(1))X<825X\begin{aligned} \#\{N\in[X,2X):N\notin\mathcal A\} &\le \Psi(2X+t-1,y_X)-\Psi(X+t-1,y_X)\\ &=\bigl(1-\log2+o(1)\bigr)X<\tfrac8{25}X \end{aligned} for all sufficiently large XX. Here Ψ(x,y)\Psi(x,y) counts the positive integers at most xx whose prime factors are all at most yy. This is an upper bound for the unassigned count, not an asymptotic equality for that count.

Proof. Let p=P(n)p=P(n) and m=n/pm=n/p. Since n>1n>1, failure of the assignment condition means either p≤2⌊X⌋p\le2\lfloor\sqrt X\rfloor or m>⌊X/2⌋m>\lfloor\sqrt X/2\rfloor. In the second case m>X/2m>\sqrt X/2, so p=nm<2(2X+t)X=yX.p=\frac{n}{m}<\frac{2(2X+t)}{\sqrt X}=y_X. The first case also gives p≤yXp\le y_X. For completeness, the classical fixed-parameter asymptotic Ψ(x,x1/u)∼xρ(u)\Psi(x,x^{1/u})\sim x\rho(u) suffices; no additional short-interval estimate is needed. Indeed, for either x=X+t−1x=X+t-1 or x=2X+t−1x=2X+t-1, log⁡yX/log⁡x→1/2\log y_X/\log x\to1/2. For every fixed 0<ϵ<10<\epsilon<1, eventually x1/(2+ϵ)≤yX≤x1/(2−ϵ).x^{1/(2+\epsilon)}\le y_X\le x^{1/(2-\epsilon)}. Monotonicity in yy bounds Ψ(x,yX)/x\Psi(x,y_X)/x between quantities tending to ρ(2+ϵ)\rho(2+\epsilon) and ρ(2−ϵ)\rho(2-\epsilon). Letting ϵ→0\epsilon\to0 and using continuity gives the limit ρ(2)\rho(2). Subtracting the two endpoint asymptotics yields (ρ(2)+o(1))X(\rho(2)+o(1))X. The Lean proof uses no smooth-number asymptotic. For large XX, yX2>2X+t−1y_X^2>2X+t-1, so an integer in (X+t−1,2X+t−1](X+t-1,2X+t-1] that is not yXy_X-smooth has exactly one prime factor above yXy_X, and Ψ(2X+t−1,yX)−Ψ(X+t−1,yX)=X−∑yX<p≤2X+t−1(⌊2X+t−1p⌋−⌊X+t−1p⌋).\Psi(2X+t-1,y_X)-\Psi(X+t-1,y_X) =X-\sum_{y_X<p\le2X+t-1} \left(\left\lfloor\frac{2X+t-1}{p}\right\rfloor -\left\lfloor\frac{X+t-1}{p}\right\rfloor\right). Mertens’ theorems, proved in Lean with explicit constants, then give (1−log⁡2)X+O(X/log⁡X)(1-\log2)X+O(X/\log X). The written proof above cites instead the fixed-uu asymptotic [20] and the value ρ(u)=1−log⁡u\rho(u)=1-\log u on [1,2][1,2] . Proposition 12.7 (The excluded-cofactor estimate). Fix h,sh,s and use the minimal admissible depth LL, as in Proposition 12.6; thus t=L−s+1=Oh,s(log⁡X)t=L-s+1=O_{h,s}(\log X). Proof. For a fixed cofactor m≤X/2m\le\sqrt X/2, each assigned index gives a prime pp with X+t≤mp<2X+tX+t\le mp<2X+t. The existence of a usable cutoff can also be made explicit by an elementary estimate.
